San Marino Was Not Made for Walking

My goal on this European Microstate trip was to truly see as much of these four tiny countries as possible in three days each. I like to walk when I travel, so this would inevitably involve lots of walking, and here is where I walked in San Marino:

Note that this doesn’t perfectly capture my walking paths because I walked down lots of random side streets and paths and I can’t remember them all.

Also note that this doesn’t perfectly capture my walking paths because I was more meandering. When I do travel walking like this, I stop for coffee in cafes, I go into stores and churches, I stop for lunch or snacks, I sit on benches and watch people, jut into woods or fields for a bit, etc. It’s a soaking process.

My three paths were not based on any established tourism routes. I roughly sketched them out ahead of time based on hitting a few key landmarks and following larger roads on my Google Maps.

What I didn’t realize until I woke up at 6 AM on Day 1 and began walking for 15 minutes is that San Marino is not made for walking. In fact, it’s among the most hostile-to-walking countries I’ve been to.

Of course, it’s easy to walk around the capital where all the tourists go, but not most of the rest of the country. It’s a land of hilly highways, most of which don’t have sidewalks, thereby often requiring me to walk through woods or farmland adjacent to the road. But sometimes the roads are wedged between, say, a rock wall and a cliff’s edge, and there was absolutely no room for pedestrians at all, and so I had to walk very slowly in the road and pray that the nice Sammarinese drivers wouldn’t swing around the sharp turns too quickly and hit me. Other times, there would be no way to safely walk along a highway on one side of the road for hundreds of yards, so to get to a wooded or farm zone on the other side of the road, I would have to frogger across fairly crowded highways.

I will generally walk anywhere when I travel, but there were two instances in San Marino when I had to turn back from my planned routes because I determined that there was literally no safe way for me to walk along a road without taking a huge risk of getting hit by a car or tumbling off a cliff.

I mean, I don’t want to exaggerate this stuff too much. The vast majority of San Marino is sparsely populated and traveled, and though the roads tend to be wide and people drive fast, there is little traffic (vehicular or pedestrian) outside the capital-to-Rimini border area, so it wasn’t like crossing the street in Kabul or whatever. But I want to emphasize that for a pleasantly boring country consisting of idyllic Italian countryside, it was surprisingly difficult simply to walk around San Marino.

My Novel Maximum Touristification Saturation Proxy

By my estimates, 99.9% of tourists who come to San Marino spend 99.9% of their waking tourist hours in the capital. It is a classic European-style old town, and I love a good European-style old town. I spent most of my first day in San Marino going to each of the Three Towers getting some of the best views in the country…

And then crisscrossing through the old town streets…

This is one of the things that makes Europe the undisputed best tourist continent in the world. America has some great cities, but there is nothing like European old towns anywhere in the States, let alone the 100 bajillion European old towns that pepper cities large and small throughout Europa.

On the other hand, San Marino’s old town reminded me of the classic tourist/traveller debates about when a city/site/place becomes overly or thoroughly touristed and ceases feeling authentic. In the above pictures, I would estimate that 99.9% of those people walking around are tourists, and that includes the people working in the stores (more on that later). Being in San Marino’s capital reminded me of a few years ago when after travelling around the Balkans for two months, I went to Dubrovnik, Croatia, and I heard nothing but American English echoing around the beautiful old town streets for days.

I think I have more tolerance for this sort of thing than a lot of travellers; I recognize that touristy sites become so touristed precisely because they are beautiful and/or fascinating. But in San Marino, I identified a good proxy for when the touristness goes too far, for when the city reaches maximum tourist saturation:

If a city, particularly an old town, starts establishing gimmicky museums that have nothing to do with the location, then it has reached the maximum touristification saturation point. It’s a sign that the city is throwing up any random bullshit that tourists might like rather than orienting its tourism around the intrinsic traits of the location.

It makes sense when specific places have specific museums dedicated to specific aspects of their cultures and history, like how Ouwerkerk, Netherlands has a flood museum, or Normandy has a D-Day Invasion Museum. It also makes sense when places have museums dedicated to more general or common practices that reflect the location’s specialization or achievements in that general practice, like how Florence has lots of art museums or London has the British Museum for archeology.

But San Marino has nothing to do with vampires or werewolves, or at least no more so than any other random European country. Maybe a city in Romania or Transylvania can get away with a museum dedicated to vampires, but IMO, the Republic of San Marino cannot.

Another example is Museums of Illusions, which, until Googling around right this very instant while writing this, I did not realize was a literal franchise. The original Museum of Illusions was built in Zagreb, Croatia in 2015, and now, as of mid-2026, ChatGPT says there are 30 Museum of Illusion franchises in Europe, plus about 10 other non-franchise Museum of Illusions-knock offs:

And Chocolate Museums (53 locations in Europe):

(Note – I exempt my excessively touristy condemnation of Chocolate Museums if they are located in countries with actual novel histories of chocolate cultivation or manufacturing [ex. Switzerland, Belgium] and are of high quality.)

A final stealth example is Museums of Torture. San Marino has one:

So does Prague:

Virtually every city in Europe has some sort of medieval history, and the general public associates medieval history with torture, so these cities can pretend that Museums of Torture are historically relevant. Where are the Sammarinese?

I have mentioned in past writing that I’m not the most sociable person in the world, but I generally at least put in a little effort to chat with some locals when I travel to a new country. Unfortunately, I found this to be impossible in San Marino.

The lady working at the front desk in my hostel was Italian. She said that she worked in San Marino because it paid better wages and was less bureaucratic than Italy.

I entered one of the 10 million tourist nicknack shops in the capital and struck up a conversation with the mid-30s guy running the store. He turned out to be from Moldova and he had lived in San Marino for 15 years but he still wasn’t a Sammarinese citizen. He said that he needed to live there for another five years before he could apply for citizenship, but otherwise loved the country.

On one of my long walks through the San Marino countryside, I stopped in a roadside café for coffee and lunch, and chatted with the waiter. He was Italian and commuted every day over the border.

I later walked into another café, this one closer to the capital but still well outside the tourist zone, and it was packed with maybe a dozen super old guys playing dominoes. Finally, I think that I found authentic Sammarinese people because I’m pretty sure old Italian men wouldn’t commute 40 minutes over the border to play dominoes in a rundown café at 10:30 AM. But the guy who brought me my coffee was Brazilian.

There must be Sammarinese somewhere in San Marino, but I scarcely saw them. Maybe one of the other workers at one of the other dozen cafes I patronized was Sammarinese? Probably the guy who politely told me in a heavy accent that I was trespassing on his farm was Sammarinese?

I dwell on this because I think I partially failed in my three-day trip in San Marino. I never actually had a conversation with a local. I underestimated the extent to which the capital area is completely dominated by tourists and how sparsely populated the rest of the country is. With 1,450 residents per square mile, San Marino is technically more densely populated than any non-microstate Western European country, but it’s still basically a bunch of villages in the Italian countryside.

The San Marino Loyalty Program and Tourist Infrastructure

I was quite impressed by San Marino’s tourist infrastructure. When travelling through the country, you get the sense that the government takes tourism seriously and whoever runs the San Marino Ministry of Tourism or whatever they have knows what they’re doing. The country is small but smooth in operation.

For instance, San Marino has not one, but two tourist loyalty programs.

I got the more basic one. Unprompted, the front desk woman at my hostel gave me a “TuttoSanMarino Card,” which gave me a 25-30% discount at almost every significant tourist site (museums, those towers, etc.) and lower discounts at most touristy restaurants in the capital, along with a few shops. There’s no sign-up, no writing down my name and address and showing my passport, just a paper card.

I pointed out to the front desk woman that my card had a three-month old expiration date.

She said it didn’t matter, that it would be accepted everywhere regardless. And she was right, no one cared and I got my discounts.

From what I gather, the point of this card is to incentivize tourists to stay overnight in San Marino, and that’s why they are handed out at hotels and the country’s one hostel. The vast majority of tourists just do day trips from Rimini, but the lure of a legitimately quite valuable 10% off most of the stuff you’re going to do in the country might get some travellers to patronize the local hotels.

What I didn’t get was the “San Marino Card,” also known as the SMaC Card, which is available to both tourists and residents. The SMaC card is accepted at most businesses in San Marino and provides cash back in the form of credit on the card at rates ranging from 2-10% per business or product (ex. 5% on tobacco, €0.20 per liter on gasoline), and then the accumulated credit can be spent at the same stores.

I think these are pretty cool ideas. The SMaC card in particular makes a lot of sense for a microstate like San Marino that gets a ton of commercial business from foreigners who shop in the country to pay lower taxes. Reward programs seem to have taken over a lot of American businesses (I can’t remember the last time I got fast food in the US without using an app) and I’m impressed that a government has seen the benefits of putting an entire country on this system.

While the loyalty programs are the standout of San Marino’s tourist structures, I want to highlight a few other bright spots.

First, there’s the aforementioned bus that runs roundtrip from Rimini to the San Marino capital all day, every hour (from about 8 AM to 7 PM). It has dozens of stops along the way where people can jump on or off, and tickets can be bought on the bus with credit cards. Oddly enough, there are allegedly other buses in San Marino, but I never saw them and couldn’t find them even when I sought them out, but I guess 99.9% of tourists just go to the capital, and the Sammarinese are all wealthy enough to have cars, so the other buses don’t matter.

Second, San Marino has free public toilets. I am on record being opposed to pay-walled public toilets despite my capitalistic inclination, so I applaud this break from European barbarism.

Third, San Marino has surprisingly good public wifi. I’ve seen public wifi all over the world, and outside of East Asia, it doesn’t work 90% of the time. But in San Marino, it does, so good for them.

Finally, San Marino has a cable car that takes people up to the top of Mount Titano to walk around the historical capital area. I highly advise any significant city with hills or mountains to have cable cars because they are virtually always one of the best parts of the city. It’s another W for San Marino.

Cars

Help me figure this out – why does San Marino have the highest rate of vehicle-ownership in the world by a large margin?

I get that San Marino, like other microstates, tends to rise to the top of these sorts of statistics due to its small population, wealth, and relatively urban landscape. But even still, San Marino beats out its fellow wealthy microstates in vehicle ownership, including the far wealthier Liechtenstein and Monaco, where I would assume everyone owns fleets of Teslas and Ferraris (respectively).

Speculative plausible explanations – San Marino is relatively wealthy, the country is sparsely populated and heavily based around roads, it has a bad bus system outside of one route, there are probably a lot of commuters to Rimini and elsewhere in Italy, and Italians generally seem to like cars (Italy has the highest rate of car ownership of any large European country).

Non-speculative contributing factor – cars are relatively cheap in San Marino. A quick glance shows VAT rates in most EU countries slap an automatic 17%-21% tax on all cars even before import duties, while San Marino has no VAT and a 17% import tax for standard cars (dropping to only 4%-8% for work vehicles).

But the tax difference isn’t that large. If anyone has any insight on why the Sammarinese are so vehicle lusted, let me know in the comments.

How Does San Marino Compete with, Integrate Into, or Engage in Regulatory/Tax Arbitrage with Italy and the European Union?

San Marino is roughly 1/4,900th the size of Italy, has roughly 1/1,700th of its population, and is completely surrounded by it. As of the summer of 2026, San Marino is also roughly 1/69,000th the size of the European Union, has roughly 1/13,200th of its population, and is completely surrounded by EU territory.

All countries must economically compete and/or integrate economically with their neighbors, but San Marino and the other European Microstates are in unique positions both to lose and benefit from their flea-on-a-beast geopolitical situations. So how does San Marino handle it?

Like the other European Microstates, San Marino is not an EU member, but it seems to have smartly used its sovereign status and microscopic geopolitical footprint to negotiate with the EU to pick and choose EU policies it wants while legally ignoring potential EU obligations. So San Marino is in a customs union with the EU, uses the Euro, has open borders with EU members, and has automatic financial information exchange with the EU (ex. if a German opens a bank account in San Marino, the republic automatically shares his financial info with German regulators). But San Marino doesn’t contribute to the EU budget, doesn’t have the EU VAT tax (15% minimum), doesn’t follow EU fiscal rules, can set its own resident quotas (ie. doesn’t have to let in 10 million Bulgarians [I kid, Bulgarians are wonderful]), and doesn’t have to abide by the infinite and ever amassing morass of EU regulations on every facet of existence, like bans on compostable plastic forks.

Or rather, all of the above paragraph was true until I was writing this essay. In October 2026, San Marino signed a new agreement with the EU that brought it far closer into its orbit. The details are generally too technical to go into, but it basically amounts to San Marino being economically integrated into the EU in all but name, except for its immigration policy. And under this new agreement, San Marino has to ban compostable plastic forks, so there goes that joke.

Most of Italy’s economic policy-making regarding San Marino is offloaded onto the EU, but there are still separate Italy-San Marino agreements regarding standardized cross-border invoicing, social security contributions, corporate dividends, etc., most of which are pretty in-the-weeds and technical.

More interestingly, when it comes to tax differentials between San Marino and Italy, the microstate seems to be engaging in some minor arbitrage to its benefit. The following is an overview with many figures rounded or simplified because taxes are always needlessly insanely complicated:

So San Marino isn’t exactly a tax haven, but its tax regime is on the lower side of the EU and is better than Italy’s, particularly its income tax and lack of VAT.

But what about the canone doganale? Isn’t Italy supposed to be bribing San Marino to not leverage its sovereignty for tax arbitrage opportunities?

For much of San Marino’s history, the canone doganale made up about half of the San Marino government’s annual revenue, but today the annual payment is… €4.65 million. There is a decent chance that there are people reading this blog who have higher annual salaries.

The most recent canone doganale negotiation was signed in 1984 and set the annual rate at 9 billion Italian lire, where it has remained ever since. In 2025, the San Marino government’s total revenue was €718.55 million, making the canone doganale about 0.6%.

From what I can tell, the relative value of canone doganale payments declined because San Marino’s government modernized and began collecting sufficient tax revenue from conventional sources (ex. income taxes) and because San Marino is conservative enough and has good enough relations with Italy and the EU to not try any crazy hardcore tax haven stuff. As for why Italy keeps paying any annual canone doganale year-after-year, my best guess is that the sum is so small that no one cares enough to stop it.

I looked for studies or analyses that indicated that San Marino was profiting off regulatory/tax arbitrage, but I couldn’t find anything significant, at least nothing contemporary. In the early 2010s, after the 2008 Global Recession annihilated San Marino’s banking system, there were some IMF/EU reports that found Italian citizens avoiding Italian/EU banking rules and taxes by dumping their assets in San Marino, but the subsequent financial reforms pretty much ended all that.

My conclusion is that San Marino is barely, if at all, playing the microstate economic arbitrage game. Its citizens are a little wealthier than Italian citizens on average and pay a little lower taxes, but are mostly integrated into the wider Italian/EU marketplace. Interestingly, as of 2003, San Marino receives almost 9,000 workers from Italy daily, constituting 45% of private sector workers, while about 1,000 Sammarinese work in Italy.

Gun Stores

While walking around San Marino on my first day, I was surprised to find a conspicuous gun store (see above). Over the next few days, I saw a lot more of these stores, both in the touristy area at the capital and in the commercial area near the Rimini border. A quick look at Google Maps finds about 15-20 gun stores in the tiny Republic of San Marino.

What’s going on here? Is San Marino the low-key Texas of Europe when it comes to guns?

Nope, nothing that fun.

For one, the vast majority of guns sold in these stores aren’t lethal firearms, they’re airsoft guns, pellet guns, replica guns, blank-firing guns, decorative guns, and some tacticool accessories. From what I gather, San Marino has moderately looser real gun regulations than Italy and most other Western European countries, but it’s still quite strict by American standards.

Maybe the gun stores are a product of regulatory arbitrage? Perhaps San Marino allows the sale of more/better/stronger non-lethal guns than Italy?

This is slightly true – for instance, San Marino permits the sale of more powerful airsoft guns than Italy – but doesn’t have much explanatory power. The problem is that Italian law doesn’t allow Italians to purchase guns-that-are-illegal-in-Italy outside of Italy and then bring them back into Italy, so the regulatory difference doesn’t provide too much commercial benefit to the republic.

The boringer explanations for San Marino’s many gun stores are:

Non-lethal guns are one of many commercial sectors that San Marino specializes in because it has lower sales/VAT taxes than Italy Some enterprising individuals set up the first gun store in the republic all the way back in 1965, and another enterprising local opened the first airsoft gun store back in 1990, before the hobby got big in Europe, so San Marino has a more developed local non-lethal gun industry than most European countries/cities It’s a novelty for European tourists who aren’t used to seeing gun stores The Shinto Shrine

Nestled not too far off the main road in the north-center of San Marino is the San Marino Jinja, or Shinto shrine, along with a memorial for the March 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami, which killed almost 20,000 Japanese and caused the Fukushima nuclear powerplant disaster. The shrine was built in Japan after the earthquake, shipped to San Marino, and reassembled there. It’s a nice show of solidarity and support between two distant peoples, and the shrine itself is pretty cool:

But I couldn’t help but wonder why this thing was in San Marino. What does the tiny 35,000-citizen European Republic of San Marino have to do with the 120 million-citizen East Asian Japan?

Maybe the two countries have some sort of special economic relationship?

Nope. In 2012, San Marino exported €6.53 million worth of goods to Japan and imported about €2.4 million from Japan. Even for San Marino, that’s not a lot for its $2.25 billion economy.

Maybe there are a lot of immigrants/emigrants between Japan and San Marino?

Nope, not that either. According to public records, in 2024, there were seven Japanese nationals living in San Marino and four Sammarinese living in Japan.

So why does San Marino have a special Japanese shrine to commemorate a Japanese disaster, as opposed to an Indonesian memorial for its 2004 tsunami, or a Bangladeshi memorial for its 2009 Cyclone Aila, or a Nepali memorial for its 2015 earthquake, etc.

The answer is… a Sammarinese weaboo.

Even in the United States, the most important country on earth, most diplomats have very little to do. The ambassadors and diplomats assigned to China or Germany or comparably geopolitically important countries have a lot to do, and therefore such posts are highly coveted, but most U.S. ambassadorships have very little to do and are so unimportant that they are pawned off as spoils and political gifts. Like, the Ambassador to Belize from 2022 to 2025 was Michelle Kwan, an Olympic figure skater who had never been to Belize, has no Belize (or Caribbean) heritage, and knew nothing about Belize. Likewise, the Ambassador to Iceland from 2019 to 2021 was a Republican donor dermatologist who had never been to Iceland and had absolutely no political experience.

My speculation is that there are probably few people with less work to do in the world than the San Marino Ambassador to Japan, but San Marino happened to have one who took his role more seriously than anyone could or should expect.

When Manlio Cadelo was a young man studying in Paris, he became friends with a Japanese exchange student and was set on a path of Japanophilia. He attended the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, moved to Japan in 1975 to work as a journalist, began working at the San Marino consulate in Japan in the late 1980s, wrote two books about Japan (in Japanese), was appointed the official Ambassador to Japan in 2002, and was promoted to “Dean of the Diplomatic Corps in Japan” in 2011.

One might suspect that Cadelo capitalized on the 2011 earthquake and tsunami to manifest his love for Japan in physical form back home in San Marino by building a Shinto shrine, but that’s not entirely accurate. Plans for building a Shinto shrine in San Marino started all the way back in 2007; the 2011 disaster only seemed to accelerate the plans, particularly the funding, which came from the sale of “Japan–San Marino Friendship Charity Gold Coins.”

I know my tone is somewhat flippant, but I find this to be a cute story. The San Marino Jinja was the brainchild of a San Marino government diplomat, but it was built with private funding on private land with no input from the government or taxpayers of San Marino or Japan besides some time commitment from an unimportant diplomat. (The government of San Marino even put out a press release before the shrine was unveiled saying that it wasn’t involved in the project and didn’t spend a Euro on it.) A Sammarinese man with an unusual but apparently earnest and enormous love for Japan managed to bring a little piece of Nippon back to San Marino. Since its opening in 2014, it’s become an admittedly remote and rarely seen but cool part of San Marino’s tourism portfolio.

What Are These Weird Gambling Machines Everywhere in Europe?

On my first day in San Marino, I woke up at 5:30 AM due to jet lag, left my hostel at 6:30 AM to walk around, and stopped at 7:30 AM at a cafe for a cappuccino (X2) and some phone scrolling. At 8:30 AM, I noticed a lady who must have been in her 60s pounding espressos and pressing buttons on a machine in a dark, dusty corner of the room. I had seen these machines before across Europe, but there was something striking about this particular display of early morning degeneracy.

They’re called gaming machines or AWPs (Amusement with Prizes). They’re usually slot machines, but they can be card games or trivia or a few other varieties.

This is one of those things that I’ve been vaguely aware of because they pop up in British/Euro tv shows (the Inbetweeners and Peep Show come to mind) but they are uncanny to the American mind. Maybe something like this exists in the US in bars and cafes in Las Vegas or Reno, but otherwise, there is a (rapidly eroding) default blanket ban on gambling across most of the country. But in Europe, seemingly regardless of EU or national gambling laws, you can find these machines anywhere.

I don’t have a problem with these machines in general (though maybe little old retired Sammarinese ladies shouldn’t be using them at 8:30 AM on a Thursday); they’re just the millionth difference between American and European culture, and I want to know more about them. Are they a right-of-passage for people? Do all young Europeans, particularly young boys, yearn to get a pint at the pub and take a run at the AWP? Are their odds horrifically rigged because drunk people are bad at probabilities? Do pubs need a license to have them because of gambling laws? Is there a reason a pub can’t have 50 of them and turn itself into a de facto casino? Are they locally made or is some Japanese pachinko conglomerate behind them?

San Marino’s Asymmetric Social Mach Bands (Or Does San Marino Conspicuously Display Its Sovereignty More Than Most Countries?)

In 2014, there was a Psychological Science paper called “Asymmetrical Social Mach Bands: Exaggeration of Social Identities on the More Esteemed Side of Group Borders.” Its thesis is that entities that are only marginally members of prestigious categories tend to emphasize their membership.

One of the examples they gave was airports – in the United States, small airports with international flights were more likely to have “international” in their names and reference their “international” nature on their websites than large international airports. Everyone knows that Washington D.C.’s Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport and New York City’s LaGuardia Airport are big enough to have international flights, so these airports don’t bother promoting that fact. But at first glance, no one would necessarily guess that Watertown International Airport in Hounsfield, New York would have international flights… but it is technically a legally designated “Airport of Entry” for private and military aircraft flying into the US, so it is “international” and promotes that fact in its name.

Based on this, I came up with a hypothesis – maybe European Microstates, compared to larger countries, display more promotions of the fact that they are indeed sovereign nations. Everyone knows that France and Germany are countries; not everyone knows that San Marino and Liechtenstein are. Conspicuous displays of sovereignty could include:

Public national flags Public signage Memorials/monuments Naming conventions (not “Bob’s Petrol Station,” but “Andorra Petrol Station”)

In the case of San Marino, I would say that I saw slightly more references to the country’s independent sovereign nature within its borders than I did in typical Western European countries, like Italy or France. There weren’t too many Sammarinese flags in San Marino, but there were a lot of signs indicating national borders and a lot of stores/cafes/restaurants with “San Marino” in the title.

I’ll call this weak evidence in support of my thesis, but I’m hoping to see more conspicuous flag waving in Liechtenstein.

San Marino’s Negative “One Weird Tricks”

Try as I might, I can’t figure out who (some rationalist blogger?) came up with the one weird trick description for small, successful countries. The idea is that when it comes to national statistics, microstates or other small countries often tend to score at the top of positive metrics, and while these ranking placements say something about the quality of a country’s governance or people, we shouldn’t over-index on these stats because they tend to reflect strange quirks of these countries amplified by their small size that can’t be abstracted to general cultural/economic/governance recommendations.

For instance, San Marino has maybe the second highest life expectancy in the world at 86 years. Is this because the Sammarinese are the healthiest people on earth? Maybe, but it’s probably due to its population consisting almost entirely of longevity-prone Italians, but with higher levels of wealth, fewer immigrants (not counting Italians), and less crime compared to surrounding Italian regions.

San Marino also has the lowest childhood mortality rate on earth of 1.3 per 1,000, compared to 6.5 in the US, 3.9 in the EU (average), 2.7 in Italy, and 2.4 in Japan.

Or a more fun example – at the 2020 Tokyo Summer Olympics, San Marino won three medals, giving it a population per capita Olympic Medal winning rate of 88 medals per million people, by far the highest in the world. The US rate was only 0.335 medals per million people, and the China rate was 0.0623 medals per million people. Pathetic.

But what I’m really interested in is ways that trend is reversed. In which metrics are San Marino particularly terrible due to its microstate status?

The Sammarinese are like the eternals in Zardoz; great at living a long time but terrible at reproducing. With a 2024 birth rate of 4.2 per 1,000 residents, San Marino has the lowest birth rate on earth, beating out South Korea (4.7), Hong Kong (4.9), Ukraine (5.7), and Japan (5.7), and a European Union average of 7.9. It doesn’t help that the Sammarinese are quite old (median age of almost 50) and the young mostly migrate out of the country to Italian cities with better job prospects. Similarly, Italians may live a long time, but their birth rates are at the second-lowest in the European Union at 6.3, behind Spain (6.5), Greece (6.6), and Lithuania (6.6).

As of July 2026, San Marino is also dead last in the world in FIFA soccer international rankings at 211th place, losing out to Anguilla (a British territory), the British Virgin Islands (also a British territory), and the US Virgin Islands. The next worst sovereign nation is the Bahamas at 207th. I guess I can’t cast too much blame on a country of 33,500 mostly old people for doing badly in international soccer tournaments, especially when its closest comp of Liechtenstein is at 206th.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, at one point San Marino had the highest death and infection rate in Europe, beating out Belgium and Andorra in the two categories respectively. This is actually a little surprising to me; sure San Marino has a lot of old people, but it’s a mostly rural area and fairly geographically isolated.

But the most surprising to me of San Marino’s negative One Weird Tricks is how much it sucks at banking.

You typically think of tiny countries or Caribbean states as being very good at banking owing to being on the edge of international financial systems (though far less so these days). San Marino seemingly played this game decently well for decades and built up a large-for-its-tiny-size financial system (banking assets were more than 600% of GDP at peak) based mostly on wealthy Italian depositors dodging Italian/EU financial monitoring. But in 2008, the Italian government pressured San Marino to integrate into its financial system, which led to huge withdrawals and a decade-long slow-motion collapse of the Sammarinese banking system.

By 2020, San Marino’s four banks had a non-performing loan (NPL) rate of 63%, meaning that 63% of the value of the loans issued by these banks were not actively being repaid and would probably default. This is apocalyptically bad. At the time, right in the middle of the COVID-19 panic, the Italian rate was 4.1% and the EU rate was 2.6%. After the 2009 financial crisis, the US banking system’s NPL rate reached 5.4%. The Sammarinese government responded with bailouts, partial bank nationalization, and more reforms to avoid a complete collapse of the financial system, and it appears to have worked, bringing the NPL rate down to 53% in 2022, and 17% in 2025, which is still horrible, but not the-ATMs-don’t-work horrible.

Why is San Marino so bad at banking? Who the hell were they giving loans to?

My understanding as TLDR – San Marino’s position as a localized offshore Italian banking depository created a selection effect that attracted primarily Italian depositors and assets that were relatively underperforming; if they were performing well, they would stick to regular Italian and EU banks. In 2008, the international financial crisis hit and Italy cracked down on Sammarinese banking secrecy, both of which put tremendous strain on already substandard Italian assets, which backfired heavily on San Marino’s then-twelve banks. From 2009 to 2010 alone, Sammarinese banks lost 35% of their assets. Over much of the following decade, the banks failed to offload most of their bad assets while government regulators heavily intervened (even facilitating the consolidation of the country’s twelve banks into four), but the financial system still hit a breaking point in 2020 that was so bad that it required another massive bailout.

I don’t want to spoil the upcoming Notes on Liechtenstein, but I personally think San Marino should have, and still should, just dump tens of millions of euros on some Liechtensteiners to run their banking system.

The Empty Store Epidemic

In an earlier section, I described a chunk of San Marino as “an odd mixture of a bunch of light suburbs and strip malls built along winding hill highways” that gives the region “the feeling of roadside truck stops and strip malls.” This not particularly pleasant aesthetic is exacerbated by an apparent epidemic of empty or near-empty store fronts.

I am not the first person to notice this. I saw a few people mention it in Reddit comments and here’s a post on the r/liminalspaces subreddit about an eerie Sammarinese mall, which I also visited:

I’m not exactly sure why this is happening in San Marino. My first guess is that these empty/near-empty stores are a product of the aforementioned Sammarinese financial boom-bust cycle. From walking extensively around the country, I saw lots of commercial activity in the capital center with all the tourists, and near the Rimini border with all the Italian shoppers, but very little activity outside those zones. Most of the empty storefronts were outside these heavy-traffic zones, so maybe there was an attempt to expand San Marino’s commercial prospects, but the demand wasn’t great enough?

The Sammarinese Don’t Kill People… Unless Coke and/or Hookers are Involved

San Marino is an extremely safe country. From Googling and ChatGPT, I could only find seven recorded murders across the country’s history, occurring in 2002, 1973, 1853, 1854 (X2), and 1782 (a double murder).

But that’s not to say that the Sammarinese aren’t murdering people elsewhere.

In October 2002, San Marino citizen Enea Bruschi hit a Brazilian transwoman prostitute named Alessandra Sostenes Ferreira Fonseca with his car in Rimini, Italy, resulting in her death.

Bruschi claimed it was an accident, but the Italian police arrested him and charged him with murder. Normally, it’s difficult to prove murderous intent for vehicular homicide, but the police claimed Bruschi had gotten in an argument with Alessandra and then he ran her down with his car. As evidence, they pointed to numerous eyewitnesses, and Bruschi’s own testimony, where he admitted that he had finished work late, gotten drunk and high on coke at an Italian bar, started driving back home to San Marino, and then he accidentally hit Alessandra with his Renault 5 while looking away from the road because he was fiddling with the gear shift that had been acting up since a previous accident. Given these statements, the Italian police did not buy that Bruschi’s association with a trans Brazilian prostitute was merely in vehicular passing.

Further investigations did not bode well for Bruschi. For one, there was no problem with his car, except that the bumper had fallen off after he hit Alessandra. Worse, Alessandra’s roommate received three calls from her that night, two of which were recorded on voicemail, which presented Alessandra as being scared and running.

Given the number of news stories on this case, I guess this was the closest thing to the OJ Trial that San Marino has ever had; the legal saga extended for seven years on new charges and appeals. Bruschi was released shortly after his arrest for lack of motive evidence, then rearrested, then charged with murder, then convicted of negligent homicide (ie. manslaughter), then convicted of intentional homicide, then that was overturned, then the overturning was overturned, and finally, he was reconvicted of negligent homicide. At that point, the story is a bit hard to track, but he seemed to have served something like three or four years in prison, got released, started a beer company in San Marino, and then died mysteriously in 2019 at age 43.

The other relevant case is sketchier (from the prosecution side) and hard to find good info on because it happened in Cuba. In March 2003, four men, including San Marino citizen Gianfranco Ercolani, were charged with negligent homicide after the death of a 17 year old Cuban girl by cocaine overdose. One is left to imagine what these four gentlemen were doing with a coked up 17 year old girl. Though, surprisingly, she came from a prominent Cuban family, and so probably wasn’t a prostitute.

Ercolani’s story was that his Italian friend was for some reason hanging out with the 17 year old Cuban girl, and she ODed on coke, so the Italian brought her to Ercolani for help, and then Ercolani and his wife tried to take her to a hospital, but the legendary Cuban healthcare system wasn’t up to the task, and so she died. Ercolani tested negative for drugs.

In November 2005, after being detained in Cuba for over two years, Ercolani was convicted of negligent homicide and sentenced to eight years in a prison for foreigners. At some point, Ercolani briefly tried to flee Cuba by jumping on one of those refugee boats going to Florida, but he apparently chickened out. He was then rearrested, and the Cubans ended up throwing an extra year onto his sentence.

Fortunately for Ercolani, the San Marino diplomatic corps came to the rescue. Eventually. In August 2008, after spending about five years in Cuban detention and prisons, Ercolani was turned over to Sammarinese authorities to serve the remainder of his sentence in San Marino as its only alleged murderer. Once back home, Ercolani was soon put under a state of “semiliberty” where he could leave prison to go to work, and later, go to his house. There are probably worse ways to serve a manslaughter sentence.

Miscellaneous San Marino is the smallest country in the world by both geography and population to win an Olympic medal, an honor held by Liechtenstein until 2021. San Marino has a street named after Napoleon, “Via Napoleon Bonaparte.” This isn’t surprising given Napoleon’s historical interaction with San Marino and that there are dozens of streets in Europe named after Napoleon, plus a few more scattered ones around the world. What is more surprising is that San Marino has a street named after American President John F. Kennedy (“Viale John Fitzgerald Kennedy”) which is located quite close to the capital’s center. In September 1963, President Kennedy was kind enough to meet with a Sammarinese delegation in Washington DC, which was the first time a Sammarinese delegation had met with an American President in 44 years (President Wilson) and would be the last time such a meeting occurred for another 44 years (President Bush II). San Marino was so honored that when Kennedy was assassinated two months later, the republic named a street after him two days later. San Marino has its very own national dessert – the Torta Tre Monti, or “Three Mountain Cakes,” an allusion to its famous three towers. To be honest, I didn’t try one, because… they don’t look great. But I’m also not a fan of pistachio.

entry.title: Devvm.dev: One VM for every project
entry.content:
One VM for every project

An isolated sandbox with your project’s toolchain, ready for you or a coding agent to start coding.

Quick start # Install devvm, and Lima with it brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm

The install script in the Linux tab also works on macOS, and Installing lists its options.

1. Go to your project

Open a terminal and cd into any project folder.

2. Run devvm

devvm shows what the new VM gets. Confirm to make it, or customize it.

3. Start your agent

devvm opens a shell in the VM, whose prompt starts with (devvm), so start your agent there.

Claude Code needs your Claude login before its first start, which devvm agent login claude makes from the VM and keeps on your machine (your first VM). The next time you run devvm in the folder, it opens the same VM, and devvm tools adds an agent to a VM you already have.

What’s supported Toolchains

devvm chooses the toolchains your project’s files call for, and you can choose more when you customize a new VM or name them with --tools (toolchains).

Coding agents

Claude Code, Codex and opencode run in the VM. Choose one when you customize a new VM, or choose them for every new VM in devvm setup (coding agents).

Layers

devvm ships the docker, nix and desktop layers, which you choose when you customize a new VM, and devvm layer new creates your own custom layers you can apply to any of your VMs (layers).

Why use devvm? Developers face attacks every day, such as supply chain attacks, leaked secrets, prompt injections and rogue agents. A sandbox limits the blast radius of an attack to what’s inside it. You know you should run your code and agents in a sandbox, but most tools need configuration and setup that’s hard to get right. devvm ships with sensible defaults so you can start coding in a sandbox with a single command. Developer ready, zero config The base image comes with optional extras that you choose, such as oh-my-bash, fzf, zoxide (z), tree and tldr. Every VM gets your git name and email, so the commits made in it are authored by you or your agent. Ports forward on their own, so a dev server on :5173 in the VM opens at localhost:5173 on your machine (ports). devvm code opens the VM in VS Code over Remote-SSH (devvm code). Isolated sandbox The VM mounts your project folder at the same path. Apart from your agents’ settings from devvm’s own store, which it gets read-only, it sees nothing else in your home folder (what a VM can reach). New VMs get the allowlist network tier by default, so they reach only an allowlist of hosts, through a proxy on your machine. You can choose a looser tier, internet or open, or a stricter one, none. On macOS, devvm locks .git’s hooks and config, so the VM can’t change what git runs on your machine (.git protection). With --clone, the VM works on a clone of the repo of its own instead of your folder, so nothing in it can touch your working tree or .git, and its work reaches your repo only when you fetch it. No sandbox closes every gap, so attack vectors lists what’s left open, and staying safe lists the habits that close most of it. Ready in seconds The first VM builds a base image, and every later VM is a copy of it that starts in seconds (images). devvm builds each version of a toolchain once and shares it read-only, so all VMs use the same copy (shared tools). Made for coding agents The agent runs in the VM, so an attack on it stays in the sandbox. It gets your settings, skills and MCP servers but never your history (coding agents). On every network tier, their secrets, such as your Claude Code token and your Codex login, stay on your machine, because the VM gets placeholders and devvm’s proxy puts the real ones into its requests on the way out. Make it yours Your own layers are setup scripts that devvm builds into an image: devvm layer new mailpit starts one, and devvm --layers mailpit makes a VM with it (your own layers). devvm setup --layers gives every new VM the layers you choose, so your shell setup, aliases or dotfiles can go in a layer of your own that each VM gets unless you leave it out (extras of your own). --from starts the base image from a container image instead of Ubuntu’s, such as node:24 or your team’s own (starting from a container image). When the project has a devcontainer.json, devvm sets up its VM from the file’s container image, ports, environment and commands (devcontainer.json). FAQ What does it run on?

devvm runs on macOS and on Linux, on arm64 or x86_64. It needs Lima, which runs the VMs with Apple’s Virtualization framework on macOS and QEMU on Linux (backends). Homebrew installs Lima along with devvm, and on Linux, Lima also needs QEMU and access to /dev/kvm. Installing lists every requirement, and known limits lists what Linux hosts lack, such as .git protection.

Does the agent run on my machine?

No. You start the agent in the VM’s shell, so it runs in the VM, and you never install it on your machine. There it sees only what the VM can reach.

Is it free?

Yes. devvm is open source under the MIT license.

Start coding in a sandbox

Install devvm, then run devvm in any project folder.

entry.title: Restaurant Delivery Payment-Skimming Campaign
entry.content:
Scamwich: Inside a Restaurant Delivery Payment-Skimming Campaign

InfoHawk research has uncovered a network of 820 suspicious restaurant domains impersonating major US chains, including Jersey Mike's, Jimmy John's, Firehouse Subs, Chipotle, and Dave's Hot Chicken. Some are running sophisticated payment-skimming attacks that capture credit card information and ask customers for their bank's SMS verification codes.

When customers order food online, they expect a familiar experience: find their restaurant, choose their meal, and pay. Increasingly, criminals are exploiting that familiarity by creating convincing clones of restaurant ordering websites, right down to the original site's underlying code.

In early November 2026, InfoHawk researchers investigated a collection of suspicious websites that appear to be part of one or more coordinated restaurant impersonation and payment-skimming operations.

Across two research passes, we identified 820 domains impersonating 35 restaurant brands. Of those, 808 use the .delivery top-level domain, and the rest use .com or .shop.

The scale is concerning, but what makes these sites particularly dangerous is how convincing they can be.

These aren't ordinary fake websites

The investigation began with a suspicious domain: mlckessejersstey[.]delivery.

The site impersonated Jersey Mike's, the popular sandwich chain, and reproduced its online ordering experience.

Rather than simply displaying a crude imitation of the restaurant's website, the attackers used a more sophisticated approach: reverse-proxying the legitimate site while replacing the checkout payment form with a malicious one.

A reverse proxy can retrieve content from a legitimate website and present it to visitors under a different domain. This allows an attacker-controlled site to display genuine pages and assets while selectively modifying the parts of the experience that matter to the attacker.

In this case, the malicious checkout requested credit card information and also asked customers for the SMS verification code sent by their bank.

This is a particularly dangerous combination. Capturing a credit card number is valuable to criminals; obtaining a one-time verification code could also help them authorize fraudulent transactions, depending on how the victim's bank uses that code.

For consumers, the experience can appear nearly indistinguishable from ordering directly from the restaurant. The site looks familiar, the menu and ordering flow can behave normally, and the fraudulent payment form appears at the moment a customer expects to pay.

Importantly, this does not require the legitimate restaurant's website to have been hacked. The attackers can operate on infrastructure they control while using the authentic restaurant website as the source of the content they display.

Mostly .delivery typosquats, plus a few look-alike .com and .shop names, found across two research passes. "Seen" is the range of registration or scan dates we have for a brand's domains, all in 2026. Open a brand to see its domains.

How the attack works

Each clone is a reverse proxy: a server that sits between the victim and the real restaurant site, fetches every page from the real site as it is requested, edits it on the way through, and passes it on. Menus, prices, store hours, and the cart are live and correct, because they come from the real site. Only the payment step is replaced. Described from mlckessejersstey[.]delivery (Jersey Mike's); we believe the clones of the other brands run the same kit.

The victim arrives from a search ad

A Google Search ad imitates the restaurant's listing and shows a look-alike domain. The domain is behind Cloudflare, so its real server is hidden, and Cloudflare gives it a valid certificate automatically (Google Trust Services here), so the browser shows "Connection is secure".

Every page is fetched live from the real site

The proxy forwards each request to the restaurant's own servers, adjusting the host name and cookies, and relays the answer. The real site's headers come through (on Jersey Mike's, x-powered-by: Nuxt and Amazon CloudFront headers), which is how we could tell which paths came from the real site and which from the scammer's server.

Addresses are rewritten to keep the victim on the fake domain

The proxy replaces the brand's own host names in pages, scripts, and redirects with the fake domain, and maps each backend to a path on it, such as /__bapi__/ or /__payments__/. Store lookup, menus, login, and cart all work, because those calls go back through the proxy to the real APIs. Even the brand's own bot-detection script still runs, with its endpoints rewritten.

Three scripts are injected into every page

A script blocker patches HTMLScriptElement.prototype.src so that listed scripts never load (on Jersey Mike's, the OneTrust cookie banner and Branch, which could send phone users to the app or the real domain). _jmu() finds the real checkout payment frame and points it at /js/index.html on the fake domain; a MutationObserver puts the fake one back whenever the page restores the real one. _chkT() reads the order total from the "Place order" button every half second and saves it, so the fake form shows the right amount.

The card form is the scammer's

A few paths are answered by the scammer's server instead of the real site: /js/* (the card form and its scripts) and /payment/socket.io. The form looks like part of checkout. On submit it collects every field (card number, expiry, CVV, name, phone) and sends it, with the site name, to the operator over a live socket.io connection.

An operator gets past the bank's check live

We believe a person watching a control panel uses the card elsewhere and, when the bank challenges that payment, tells the victim's page what to show next: "card declined, try another", a page asking for the SMS code (/js/confirmation/), an "approve in your bank app" page (/js/app/), or "invalid code, try again". We believe the code the victim types is what lets the operator's charge through 3-D Secure.

The victim is sent away

When the operator marks it a success, the page sets a cookie valid=77777 lasting until 2038 and sends the victim to another chain's real site (href.li/?https://www.jimmyjohns.com/; href.li hides where they came from). No order reaches the restaurant: the real payment step never runs, so there is no confirmation email and no food. We believe the victim's card is then charged for whatever the operator bought.

Why this design. The clone never goes out of date, the victim builds a real order with a real total before anything looks wrong, and one kit works against any restaurant by changing the target site, the domain, and a few path rules. The scammer's server does very little work, which makes it cheap to move. Some variants skip the payment wording and only pin the frame's address, re-setting it every time the page changes it.

Distribution of the Delivery Scam

Searching Google's ad archive (Ads Transparency Center) for the domains in our first sweep found at least 47 Google Search text ads between July 7, 2026, and October 20, 2026, run under at least 46 separate advertiser accounts with at least 43 different, unrelated-looking business names (construction firms, a reptile rescue, a watch company). The ads below are a sub-sample: we searched only for the domains in our first sweep, so there are likely more. Each ad imitates a restaurant's search listing and shows a look-alike domain. Most ran for 1â4 days, usually starting days after the domain was registered.

Status: On November 4, 2026, 367 of the 820 domains still served a site, so they could be getting traffic through means other than ads. None of the ads below were still running on November 3, 2026, but this scam may also be running through other ads, or other means. Google's public Ads Transparency pages now show "Can't find ad" for the creatives and "No ads found" for the domains we checked, which suggests Google has taken them down; the "Ads Transparency page" links below will likely not load. Of the 47 ads below, 41 have Google's rendered image; the rest show the text from Google's ad preview. Domains in the image ads were read from the image and may contain small reading errors.

It uses the same cloning technique, but we found nothing that shows the same people run it, so these sites may come from more than one operator using the same kit.

What this means for restaurant brands

These clones don't need to break into a restaurant's systems. They borrow the real site, page by page, and insert the attack only at the moment a customer pays. That makes them hard to spot from the outside, but it also means the brand's own servers see every page the clone serves. Brands and their ordering providers that watch for their site loading under someone else's domain, or for checkout sessions that never reach the real payment provider, are well placed to catch these sites early.

entry.title: GitHub's new Git storage architecture
entry.content:
Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture

GitHub’s new Git storage architecture is built so thousands of agents can push to a single repository at once. Here’s how it works.

Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running.

Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post, we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage.

We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture.

The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components.

Building for agent scale

We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes:

Horizontal scale is how many developers and agents can work across many repositories. Many of GitHub’s current approaches on this axis have been battle-tested over the years and are carried forward to the new architecture: partitioning of tenants across infrastructure, isolation and/or fairness enforcement of tenant traffic, and load-aware routing, to name a few. Vertical scale is how many developers and agents can work on one repository. As agents write more code, we expect individual repositories to get larger and busier, so most of our requirements came from the vertical axis.

Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes.

We’re already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then.

We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to:

Accept thousands of writes per second. Support multiple writer nodes. There are two reasons for this: Experience has taught us that indexing incoming packs and checking object connectivity are the most CPU-expensive parts of a write, and that cost scales with the size of the write, so a single node will become compute-bound quickly.Spreading that work across many nodes improves fault tolerance and shortens recovery when a node fails. Minimize commit latency. An agent waits on each push before it moves to its next step. Record changes in order for each reference with the ability to quickly linearize across references. A virtual replica that falls behind needs to catch up by downloading only the data it needs to serve the incoming request. Keep reads cheap when nothing has changed, which is the common case given the read-to-write ratio. Let each component scale independently.

On top of that, the system had to be able to improve overall reliability and scale globally.

Introducing “Project Rubicon”

In May of 2026, hot on the heels of the initial Azure migration, we started working on a design that could meet those demands. We tried several approaches. In all of them, pack data lived in Azure Blob Storage, and in some we experimented with keeping reference state there too. We’ll cover some of the trade-offs we found below, but we settled on a design we felt maximized throughput while preserving the correctness, durability, availability, and latency guarantees a platform like GitHub requires. We called it “Rubicon,” a nod to the point of no return the industry crossed with agentic development.

Let’s walk through Rubicon from the top down. Many things stay the same: requests from Git clients, the API, and the web UI arrive at Spokes, which still handles routing and load balancing, and serves the internal API that the rest of GitHub uses to read and write repository data. Spokes also maintains its role as a placement and balancing service, maintaining the partitioning, isolation, and tenant fairness required for horizontal scale. The data plane underneath Spokes, in contrast, is new.

Spokes routes each request to one of a small group of virtual replicas assigned to that repository. Virtual replicas are a single fleet of disposable compute that serves reads, writes, or both. A virtual replica’s local disk is a cache that can be rebuilt at any time.

Spokes routes a repository’s traffic to the same virtual replicas when it can, which keeps their caches warm and latency low, but nothing about correctness depends on a request landing on any particular virtual replica. When a virtual replica goes away, the repository’s other virtual replicas keep serving, and a replacement fills its cache as traffic arrives.

When a repository gets busy, we add more virtual replicas. Separately, a fleet of compaction nodes works in the background, directly against Blob Storage and Ref-CAS, to merge each repository’s packs and remove unreachable objects. That work never runs on a virtual replica, meaning their CPU and memory can be almost entirely dedicated to serving requests.

Durable state lives in two places:

Git objects, in the form of packs and auxiliary read acceleration data, live in Azure Blob Storage. References and the list of packs that make up the repository (the pack manifest) live in a separate replicated log service we call Ref-CAS (for “Reference Compare-and-Swap”).

Let’s walk the architecture from the perspective of a write and a read:

Write: a virtual replica indexes the incoming pack and uploads it to Blob Storage, then commits one transaction to Ref-CAS that lists the pack in the manifest and updates the references. Later, a compaction node merges that pack with others to keep reads fast. Read: a virtual replica checks its reference version with Ref-CAS, pulls the packs it needs from Blob Storage into its cache, and serves the read from there.

There are many distinct approaches we’ve taken within the new architecture, from the software stack on the virtual replicas to how traffic routing and workload scheduling are tuned for different use cases (e.g., many small repos vs. one large one). Let’s dive deep into two components of the architecture and tell their stories centered on the two design principles.

Minimizing coordination: mutating reference state at high throughput

Object storage services like Azure Blob Storage are incredibly good at what they do, and natural fits for many data-heavy applications like source code storage. They are durable and replicated, hold as much as we need them to, have a relatively low cost per byte, and deliver exceptionally high aggregate throughput so long as traffic is spread across many keys. As a result, nearly everything durable in the new Git storage architecture lives in Azure Blob Storage, including:

Packs and indexes written by pushes, compaction, and garbage collection. Various read accelerators (like multi-pack indexes, reachability bitmaps, and some custom formats) that our maintenance process builds from those packs. Records that let compaction and garbage collection resume or audit their work, along with the leases that compaction nodes use to claim work. Cached responses for frequently repeated fetches. Checkpoints for the reference state of the repository, though not the authoritative state used to serve requests.

Most of that data is written once to a distinct key and never changes afterward, which is what makes it highly suitable for Blob Storage.

References are the opposite. A busy repository’s references are a relatively small piece of state that many writes race to update at the same time. That access pattern is harder to serve from Blob Storage, and our first prototypes showed us why. Object storage for this kind of workload is an intuitive choice, and one that works well up to a certain level of scale: conditional writes give a compare-and-swap for free, and the data is already durable and replicated. However, we ran into a difficult set of choices, illustrated below by two approaches we tried.

Our first approach was a write-ahead log for all of a repository’s references, indexed by a single blob. Every update is a conditional write against that blob. It’s correct, and reads are cheap: a virtual replica asks whether the blob has changed, and if it hasn’t, it’s done. Writes are where it falls short. Only one conditional write to a blob can be in flight at a time, so even when we batch every push that arrives during a write into the next one, the repository’s write ceiling is one write per round trip to a single blob. In practice, this netted us write throughput in the mid-hundreds per second.

Our second approach split the references across several segment blobs, with each reference hashing to one of them. Writes to references in different segments no longer wait on each other, which raises the ceiling. But a read now has to check every segment to know whether anything changed, and it’s only as fast as the slowest segment. We’d traded write latency for read latency, and reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude. We can visualize this by showing multiple writes and a read side by side:

Neither option met every requirement, so we built something else: a replicated log service dedicated to references, or the Ref-CAS service. This is the (small) consensus group we said at the end of the last post was still somewhere in the stack. Here’s how it works.

Each reference update in Ref-CAS is a compare-and-swap committed by a quorum. A transaction locks only the references it touches, checks that each one still has the value the writer expects, and becomes visible once a majority of the log’s replicas have recorded it. Agents mostly push to their own branches, so most updates don’t contend, and they replicate in parallel. When two pushes do update the same reference, only one will append to the log.

Each commit to Ref-CAS gets a log sequence number (LSN), and the repository’s version is the LSN of its latest commit. Reads start with a version check against that version. A virtual replica sends the version of the reference state it already holds. If that version is still current, the reply carries no references at all, and an unchanged repository costs a single comparison. If the virtual replica is behind, it gets back the current references and version, along with pointers to pack data and anything else that needs to be known, such as when the last garbage collection cycle occurred.

Unlike the consensus group in our legacy architecture, Ref-CAS never holds or validates object data. It only stores pointers to it. A virtual replica uploads a push’s pack to Blob Storage before it commits the reference transaction. A reference only ever points at objects that are already durable.

These approaches allow us to transact reference state alone in the tens of thousands of operations per second, and provide a baseline for additional annotations on the replication log that help reads decide what to download for a given request.

But supporting thousands of writes per second on a single repository creates a second-order problem: maintaining the performance of reads and writes. For that, we needed a different approach to compaction.

Decoupling storage from compute: compaction at thousands of writes per second

Every push adds a pack to Blob Storage. Git can serve a repository from many packs, but each additional pack makes lookups slightly more expensive, so the pack count can’t grow without bound. In our legacy architecture, compaction runs on the same replicas that serve traffic, and it has to run on every replica. In the new architecture, it runs entirely in the background on separate nodes, directly against durable storage, using the Ref-CAS service to notify virtual replicas of the evolving state.

Compaction nodes each claim ownership over a subset of the repository’s data via a lease, which allows us to scale compaction horizontally. Here’s how one compaction node works through a single shard of a repository’s packs:

The node first takes a lease on the shard in Blob Storage, so only one node compacts a shard at a time. Meanwhile, virtual replicas keep uploading packs and listing them in the pack manifest. The node reads the manifest to find new packs and collects them into an open segment, which is effectively a holding ground for data about to be compacted. When the segment reaches a defined limit based on pack count, size, or age, it seals the segment so it accepts no new packs, then combines its packs into fewer, larger ones. While compaction happens, the next segment for the shard can begin capturing its input packs. Before anything is published, the node checks that the new packs contain exactly the same objects as the inputs. It then uploads the new packs and adds them to the manifest. A second transaction removes the inputs from the manifest, and cleanup deletes them later.

To scale out, this process runs independently for many shards at once. Each pack’s hash maps to a shard, so adding shards and nodes adds compaction throughput. A compacted pack that’s still under the size limit goes back into a shard by its own hash and merges again, so packs grow in tiers until they reach the limit. The net result is an effectively flat pack count while pushes climb:

Compaction merges packs, but it keeps every object. Garbage collection is the step that removes objects nothing references anymore, like the ones left behind by deleted branches and force-pushes. In our new architecture, garbage collection works very similarly to compaction by using dedicated workers to handle the compute-heavy portion. It also has a few special behaviors for safely removing data, which are worthy of their own discussion.

Using these approaches, we’ve been able to consistently demonstrate a flat latency curve as writes climb, and we have other planned optimizations to make the compaction and garbage collection processes themselves more performant.

What comes next

The two principles we started with let each part of this architecture scale on its own. We scale reads and writes by adding virtual replicas. Ref-CAS orders each reference independently instead of the whole repository. We scale maintenance by adding compaction nodes. Our goal is for every repository, from one developer’s side project to the busiest monorepo, to run on the same architecture with no special handling for the busy ones. Repositories don’t stay small. A side project can pick up a fleet of agents overnight, and it shouldn’t need a migration or special handling from us to keep up. One architecture also means every improvement we make reaches every repository at once.

This foundation lets us do a lot more. We’re focused on three areas next: scaling the architecture beyond what we can predict we’ll need today, making agents more efficient at the work they do on GitHub, and evolving Git itself for agentic development.

Improving the architecture

We have plans to take this architecture further. Each of these improvements lets a repository handle more activity while reducing the work behind each request:

Read only what’s needed. Fetch a single object from Blob Storage instead of the whole pack that holds it. Organize packs by type. Group commits, trees, and blobs into their own packs. Many requests then touch less data. Partial replicas. Serve requests without every pack on local disk. Materialized views. Keep repository data in ready-to-use forms, like prepared archives, a near-live shallow copy of the default branch, and agent session context stored alongside each commit. Global replicas. Place replicas in any region, close to the workloads that use them. Reads stay within bounded staleness of the latest write. Scale to zero. Grow and shrink the fleet with the repositories that are actually active. Efficient agent operations on GitHub

Scaling the infrastructure is one side of supporting agents. The other side is making each agent operation cheaper: fewer bytes to fetch, fewer round trips, and less waiting on changes. Each of these fast-follow items builds on the storage work in this post:

Work without a clone. Many agent tasks never need a full working tree. They need a handful of files and enough context to make a change. They can read both straight from the server. Atomic commit API. Land a multi-file change in one operation. The whole change commits, or it’s rejected cleanly on conflict. Event streams. Agents and the systems around them work best with real-time information. A generic event stream lets them subscribe to changes and react as they happen. Improving Git for agents

We also have work to do in Git itself. GitHub has been a longtime contributor to the Git project, and we’re not stopping now. A few examples of the work we’re excited to continue:

Lightweight clones. Partial clone, shallow clone, and sparse checkout each let an agent fetch less. Each one has gaps. They don’t always work well together, either. We want to improve each piece and make them fit. Remove hidden scaling costs. Git still has code paths that slow down much faster than the repository grows. Recent releases fixed several of them, but we expect to find more. Faster history walks. Metadata like the commit-graph can answer merge-base and reachability questions without walking every commit. That matters most when an agent’s API call turns into Git work on the server. Avoid common gotchas. Agents make the same mistakes developers do. Git can catch more of the common ones and warn before they cause damage.

Agents have changed how software gets built. GitHub and Git are changing with it. We’re excited to take this new architecture across the starting line. It’s available in a limited private preview now, with a broader rollout early next year. We can’t wait to see what teams build when the number of agents working on a repository is limited by their ideas. We’ll keep evolving Git and GitHub alongside our customers and the Git community.
